The landlord's story about a 'burst pipe' gained no credence once we found the water bill hadn't changed in six months.

meanings.en: a tendency to believe things too readily, without enough evidence; gullibility
meanings.zh: 轻信;易受骗;缺乏辨别力

examples: The scammer preyed on her credulity, convincing her over three phone calls that her bank account had been hacked by 'federal agents.'
That the app promises to double your investment in a week strains credulity, yet thousands of people still wire money to it every month.
Advertisers count on a certain amount of credulity — nobody actually believes the cream erases wrinkles overnight, but enough people buy it anyway.

meanings.en: deserving blame for a wrong or failure

examples: The internal audit found the manager culpable for approving three months of falsified expense reports without ever checking a single receipt.
If the self-driving car's software ignored a known bug, is the engineer who shipped the update legally culpable for the accident?
She felt culpable for missing the red flags in her college roommate's spending, even though the credit card fraud wasn't remotely her fault.

meanings.en: hasty and superficial; done quickly without attention to detail
meanings.zh: 粗略的;草率的;走马观花的

examples: He gave the 40-page contract only a cursory glance before signing, and later discovered a clause auto-renewing his gym membership for two years.
The recruiter's cursory review of my resume — eleven seconds, according to LinkedIn's own analytics — decided whether I got an interview.
A cursory scroll through the apartment photos hid the mold in the bathroom, which only showed up during the in-person walkthrough.

meanings.en: behavior in keeping with good taste and propriety; polite formality

examples: Even after the Zoom call turned into a shouting match about the missed deadline, the CFO maintained perfect decorum and never once raised his voice.
Wearing pajama bottoms to a client dinner, even a virtual one, breaks every rule of workplace decorum HR ever wrote down.
Grandma still insists on decorum at the dinner table — phones face down, elbows off the tablecloth, no scrolling during dessert.

meanings.en: moving from topic to topic without a clear plan; rambling
meanings.zh: 东拉西扯的;散漫的;不着边际的

examples: The standup meeting that's supposed to take ten minutes turned into a 45-minute discursive ramble about someone's weekend hiking trip.
Her podcast is delightfully discursive — she'll start reviewing a ramen shop and somehow end up telling you her grandmother's immigration story.
The therapist gently steered him back on track every time his answers drifted into discursive tangents about his coworkers.

meanings.en: tending to control others in an unpleasant, overbearing way

examples: Her domineering manager rewrote every Slack message before it went out, then took full credit for the campaign in the quarterly review.
He quit the startup after eight months under a domineering co-founder who scheduled 7 a.m. calls just to prove who was in charge.
Their domineering mother still calls to approve the paint colors in their new apartment, three states away.

meanings.en: (of a disease or species) regularly found in a particular area or group, often hard to eradicate
meanings.zh: (疾病、物种等)某地区特有的;地方性的,难以根除的

meanings.en: (of a problem) persistently and widely present within a particular group or system
meanings.zh: (问题)普遍存在的;根深蒂固的

examples: Burnout is practically endemic in the startup world, where 'we're a family' usually means unpaid overtime and no sick days.
Dengue fever is endemic to parts of Southeast Asia, so the travel clinic recommended repellent and long sleeves before our Bali trip.
Ghost jobs — listings companies never intend to fill — have become endemic on LinkedIn, wasting thousands of applicants' hours every week.

meanings.en: a person who takes particular pleasure in fine food and drink; a gourmet

examples: My roommate the epicure spent forty minutes comparing three olive oils before deciding which one deserved to go on our six-dollar pasta.
The app's algorithm now sorts restaurants by an 'epicure score,' which apparently just means how many truffle shavings they add to everything.
He's turned into a real epicure since moving to Portland, texting me photos of foraged mushrooms he's about to braise for dinner.

meanings.en: well-suited to the occasion, especially in expression; apt or fortunately timed
meanings.zh: (言辞、举动)恰如其分的;贴切巧妙的;时机凑巧的

examples: Her toast at the wedding was so felicitous that even the bride's notoriously cynical uncle got misty-eyed.
Naming the budgeting app 'Copilot' turned out to be a felicitous choice — it launched right as everyone started comparing every product to an AI assistant.
It was almost felicitous timing: he got the job offer the same morning his lease renewal was due, so he didn't have to decide twice.

meanings.en: having or showing passionate intensity of feeling

examples: She's a fervent believer in the four-day workweek and will corner you at any party to explain the productivity data.
His fervent apology in the group chat — three paragraphs, two crying emojis — didn't stop everyone from muting the thread anyway.
Fans lined up outside the stadium at dawn, fervent in their hope that this was finally the season the team wouldn't choke.

meanings.en: intense and passionate feeling, especially in support of a cause or belief

examples: The new hire pitched the rebrand with such fervor that the whole meeting forgot to ask whether anyone actually wanted a rebrand.
Fans queued outside the pop-up store with the fervor usually reserved for concert tickets, just to buy a limited-edition phone case.
Her fervor for the volunteer project faded fast once she realized 'flexible hours' meant every Saturday morning for a year.

meanings.en: to make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing; to provide evidence against

examples: He deleted the group chat the moment the investigation started, which only made the messages look more incriminating in hindsight.
Employees are told never to write anything in email that could incriminate the company later — 'put it on a call' is basically corporate law.
The dashcam footage ended up incriminating the other driver, who had told the insurance company a completely different story.

meanings.en: to accuse of or show involvement in a fault or crime

examples: The intern's forwarded Slack messages ended up inculpating the whole marketing team in the leaked-campaign scandal, not just the one person who sent it.
His lawyer advised him to stay silent in the interview, since anything he said could inculpate him further in the fraud case.
The audit was careful not to inculpate the entire finance department when only one rogue approver had signed off on the fake invoices.

meanings.en: (law) behavior or material that is offensive to accepted standards of morality, especially of a sexual nature
meanings.zh: (法律)猥亵;不雅行为;有伤风化

examples: The prosecutor charged him with public indecency after witnesses reported the incident near the elementary school.
The broadcasting regulator fined the station for indecency after the uncensored clip aired during the afternoon time slot.

meanings.en: (typesetting) to start a line of text further from the margin than the rest of the paragraph
(chiefly British/business) an official order for goods, especially placed with a foreign supplier

examples: The linter kept failing until I indented the nested JSX block by two more spaces.
Procurement raised an indent for three hundred server racks, routing it straight to the Shenzhen supplier.

meanings.en: to formally charge with or accuse of a serious crime

examples: The federal grand jury voted to indict the former executive on eleven counts of wire fraud after the whistleblower's emails surfaced.
The documentary doesn't just tell his story — it quietly indicts an entire industry that looked the other way for a decade.
Prosecutors said they had enough evidence to indict him for insider trading the moment the SEC subpoenaed his text messages.

meanings.en: a scheming or crafty plot, often secret, intended to accomplish some usually harmful end

examples: It took a whistleblower and eighteen months of leaked memos to expose the board's machinations to oust the founder without triggering a stock crash.
Behind the friendly all-hands presentation lay months of quiet machinations — reorgs planned, layoffs budgeted — that nobody on the floor knew about yet.
The reality show thrives on petty machinations: alliances built over cocktails, then broken the second someone gets a rose.

meanings.en: occurring at a time that is suitable or advantageous

examples: She quit her job the week before the company's stock crashed — either incredibly opportune timing or she knew something the rest of us didn't.
Landing at exactly the moment his flight was delayed felt opportune; we grabbed coffee together instead of missing each other by an hour.
The venture fund waited for the most opportune moment in the news cycle to announce the acquisition, right after a rival's product recall.

meanings.en: more important than anything else; supreme

examples: In the pre-op briefing, the surgeon reminded the whole team that patient safety was paramount, above any pressure to finish the schedule on time.
For a first-time homebuyer, reading the inspection report is paramount — skip it and you might inherit a thirty-thousand-dollar foundation problem.
During the acquisition talks, keeping the deal secret from the press was treated as paramount, even more urgent than finalizing the price.

meanings.en: carried out with minimum effort or reflection, as a mere routine duty
meanings.zh: 敷衍了事的;例行公事的;草率的

examples: The manager's perfunctory 'great job, team' at the end of every meeting stopped meaning anything after the third round of layoffs.
His performance review was so perfunctory — two lines, clearly copy-pasted from last year — that he wondered if his boss remembered his name.
She gave the smoke detector a perfunctory tap instead of actually testing the battery, and of course it died during the actual fire.

meanings.en: the process of obtaining goods, services, or supplies, especially for an organization

examples: The procurement department took six weeks to approve a forty-dollar standing desk, but somehow signed off on a two-hundred-thousand-dollar software contract in two days.
After the chip shortage, the company overhauled its procurement strategy, diversifying suppliers instead of relying on a single factory overseas.
Public procurement rules meant the city had to accept three competing bids before it could even repaint the crosswalks.

meanings.en: having or showing a strong desire for revenge; spiteful

examples: After she reported him to HR, he got vindictive and started quietly excluding her from every meeting invite he controlled.
The ex left a string of one-star reviews on her new boyfriend's small business, which felt less like feedback and more like a vindictive campaign.
The coach benched the player for the whole season over one late arrival — the team called it discipline, but it looked vindictive to everyone watching.

meanings.en: behavior, speech, or manner that is artificial and adopted to impress others

examples: His British accent turned out to be pure affectation — he grew up in Ohio and picked it up after one semester abroad.
Ordering the omakase and photographing every single course felt less like appreciation and more like affectation for the Instagram grid.
She dropped the fake enthusiasm and corporate jargon the moment the camera stopped rolling, as if the whole meeting had been an affectation.

meanings.en: (medicine) the use of drugs to induce a loss of sensation or consciousness during a medical procedure

examples: The anesthesiologist adjusted the general anesthesia dosage the moment the patient's heart rate spiked on the monitor.
She opted for local anesthesia so she could stay awake and chat through the entire wisdom-tooth extraction.
Post-op nausea is common after general anesthesia, so the nurse kept a basin within reach for the first hour.

meanings.en: shameless and undisguised, especially in wrongdoing
meanings.zh: 厚颜无耻的;明目张胆的

examples: Claiming he'd 'never received' the invoice, right after replying to it twice, was a barefaced lie and everyone on the call knew it.
Copying her coworker's entire slide deck and presenting it as her own idea the next morning was a barefaced act of theft.
The barefaced audacity of charging a 'resort fee' at a motel next to the highway made the whole checkout process feel like a scam.

meanings.en: making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible; favorable to

examples: An open-plan office with constant Slack pings is not exactly conducive to the deep focus the job actually requires.
Doctors say a consistent bedtime and no phone in the room are far more conducive to good sleep than any melatonin gummy.
The landlord's decision to allow pets and add a rooftop garden made the building far more conducive to actually meeting your neighbors.

meanings.en: to cause someone to lose loyalty or affection, making them discontented or rebellious

examples: Three rounds of unpaid overtime and a canceled bonus were enough to disaffect even the most loyal engineers on the team.
The sudden return-to-office mandate disaffected employees who had relocated across the country during two years of remote work.
Constant last-minute schedule changes gradually disaffected the part-time staff, and half of them quit within the same month.

meanings.en: to give someone or something a higher moral or dignified quality; to elevate

examples: Volunteering at the shelter every Sunday didn't make him rich, but he said it ennobled the rest of his week in a way his job never did.
The documentary tries to ennoble the gig-economy delivery driver as a modern folk hero, though most of them would just rather get paid more.
Surviving chemo together seemed to ennoble their marriage, stripping away years of petty arguments about whose turn it was to do dishes.

meanings.en: to praise highly in speech or writing, especially someone who has died
meanings.zh: (尤指在葬礼上)颂扬;称颂;赞美

examples: At the retirement party, three coworkers took turns eulogizing a manager none of them had actually enjoyed working for.
Tech journalists rushed to eulogize the founder's 'visionary genius' within hours of the IPO, conveniently forgetting the two startups that failed before it.
Her brother eulogized their grandfather with stories nobody in the family had heard before, and the whole room was in tears by the end.

meanings.en: the act of freeing someone or something from a difficulty, constraint, or entanglement

examples: His extrication from the failing startup took a lawyer, a messy non-compete negotiation, and four months of awkward silence in the group chat.
Firefighters spent nearly an hour on the extrication of the driver, who was pinned when the car folded around the guardrail.
Getting out of the timeshare contract required a full year of paperwork; the extrication cost almost as much as the vacations it was meant to fund.

meanings.en: treating serious issues with deliberately inappropriate humor; flippant
meanings.zh: 轻浮的;不合时宜地开玩笑的;油腔滑调的

examples: When his manager asked why the deploy broke production, he made a facetious joke about 'moving fast and breaking things,' which did not land well.
I wasn't being facetious when I said the rent was insane — I genuinely checked four apps and it's $2,800 for a studio.
Her facetious reply to the layoff announcement, something about 'finally getting that gap year,' didn't go over well in the all-hands chat.

meanings.en: lacking efficiency, competence, or a sense of responsibility; ineffective
meanings.zh: 无能的;不负责任的;软弱无力的

examples: The feckless project manager missed every deadline and blamed 'communication issues' on a team that communicated constantly.
Critics called the mayor feckless for promising to fix the subway across three campaigns while nothing about the commute actually changed.
Her feckless roommate kept 'meaning to' pay his share of the rent, three months running, until she finally changed the locks.

meanings.en: impossible to remove, erase, or forget; permanent
meanings.zh: 不可磨灭的;去不掉的;难忘的

examples: The toddler left an indelible red marker streak across the new couch within twenty minutes of getting it as a gift.
Watching her grandmother cook that last Lunar New Year dinner left an indelible memory she still tries to recreate every winter.
One brutal one-star review, quoted in every pitch meeting since, left an indelible mark on how the founders talk about the product.

meanings.en: to make physically hard, or to make emotionally hardened and unfeeling through repeated exposure
physically hardened, or emotionally hardened and unfeeling
meanings.zh: (身体或情感上)变硬的;麻木不仁的

examples: Years of empty promises and surprise layoffs had indurated the veteran employees, who now read every 'exciting update' email with total cynicism.
Decades on the boats had indurated the fisherman's hands until calluses replaced any softness left in his palms.
He seemed indurate to the customers' complaints, nodding along in the review meeting without changing a single process afterward.

meanings.en: to overwhelm someone with a large number of things to deal with, or to flood a place with water
meanings.zh: (以大量事物)淹没;充斥;(洪水)淹没

examples: The moment the layoff rumor hit social media, the HR inbox was inundated with over three hundred anxious emails in a single afternoon.
Monsoon rains inundated the coastal village, and by morning our host family's ground floor was under two feet of water.
New parents get inundated with unsolicited advice the second the pregnancy announcement goes up, half of it contradicting the other half.

meanings.en: (mathematics/philosophy) unable to be reduced, simplified, or broken down into a simpler or smaller form
meanings.zh: (数学/哲学)不可约的;不可简化的

examples: The professor proved the polynomial was irreducible over the rationals, meaning it couldn't be factored into smaller pieces.
Consciousness, the philosopher argued, is an irreducible property that no amount of neuroscience alone can fully explain.
After three rounds of budget cuts, the finance team said the remaining costs were irreducible without shutting down the lab.

meanings.en: stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or course of action despite pressure to do so
meanings.zh: 顽固的;执拗的;不为所动的

examples: The landlord stayed obdurate about the rent increase even after half the building threatened to move out at once.
No amount of user data about the failed feature could move the obdurate product lead, who insisted people 'just needed to get used to it.'
Her parents remained obdurate about the wedding venue, refusing to even look at the budget spreadsheet she'd spent a week building.

meanings.en: able to perceive or feel things through the senses; conscious and capable of experience
meanings.zh: 有感觉能力的;有知觉的;有意识的

examples: The debate over whether the chatbot is sentient resurfaces every time it says something unsettlingly self-aware in a customer support chat.
Watching the octopus at the aquarium solve the jar puzzle, my nephew asked if it was as sentient as our dog.
The new AI ethics course spends a whole week on how we'd even prove a machine were sentient rather than just very good at mimicry.

meanings.en: a natural liking, sympathy, or attraction for someone or something
meanings.zh: 天然的喜爱;亲近感;吸引力

meanings.en: a close similarity, structural resemblance, or connection between things
meanings.zh: (事物间的)相似性;关联;(化学)亲和力

examples: She'd always had an affinity for spreadsheets, the kind of person who color-coded her budget for fun.
The two founders had an instant affinity, finishing each other's sentences by the second coffee meeting.
Chemists study the affinity between the drug molecule and the receptor to predict how well it binds.

meanings.en: an open and deliberate insult or act of disrespect
to insult or offend someone openly and deliberately

examples: Being seated at the intern table felt like a personal affront to the VP, who left before dessert.
She took his unsolicited feedback on her code as an affront, even though he meant it kindly.
Skipping her promotion announcement in the all-hands email affronted her more than the raise itself would have pleased her.

meanings.en: to charm or enchant someone, often in a deceptive or misleading way
meanings.zh: (常以欺骗手段)迷惑;哄骗;吸引

meanings.en: to make time pass pleasantly; to help while away time

examples: The startup's slick demo beguiled investors so completely that nobody asked about the burn rate.
He beguiled his Tinder date with stories that later turned out to be someone else's LinkedIn achievements.
We beguiled the six-hour layover playing cards and comparing terrible airport food.

meanings.en: modest or shy because one lacks confidence in oneself
meanings.zh: 缺乏自信的;羞怯的;拘谨的

examples: He was diffident about sharing his idea in the meeting, mumbling it almost as an apology before someone else took credit.
Despite acing the interview, she stayed diffident about her chances and refused to tell anyone she'd applied.

meanings.en: (medicine) a disorder in which an organ or tissue wastes away, especially due to poor nourishment or a genetic defect

examples: The neurologist explained that muscular dystrophy gradually weakens the muscles because the body can't produce enough dystrophin.
The geneticist screened the newborn for early markers of dystrophy after two older siblings were diagnosed with it.

meanings.en: insolent or shameless boldness; disrespectful audacity

examples: He had the effrontery to ask for a raise the same week he missed three deadlines.
She screenshotted his message and posted it, stunned by the sheer effrontery of asking to borrow money twice.

meanings.en: a widely held but mistaken belief, often based on flawed logic
meanings.zh: 谬误;似是而非的观点(区别于 fallible‘会犯错的’、infallible‘绝不出错的’)

examples: It's a common fallacy that multitasking makes you more productive — studies keep showing the opposite.
The landlord's argument rested on the fallacy that a higher rent automatically means a better tenant.

meanings.en: capable of making errors or being wrong; not infallible
meanings.zh: 会犯错误的;不可靠的(区别于 fallacy‘谬误’这一名词)

examples: Even the AI model everyone trusted turned out to be fallible, confidently citing a court case that never existed.
Remember your doctor is fallible too — get a second opinion before agreeing to surgery.

meanings.en: faithfulness or loyalty to a person, cause, or commitment
the degree of exactness with which something, especially sound or data, is reproduced
meanings.zh: (音频、数据等的)保真度;精确度

examples: After the affair came out, the whole group chat debated whether fidelity even matters in a long-distance relationship.
He swore fidelity to the startup's mission, then quietly interviewed at three competitors that same month.
The new earbuds promise studio-level fidelity, but honestly I can't hear the difference on the subway.

meanings.en: to prevent or delay an event or action by acting first
meanings.zh: 预先阻止;先发制人地防止

examples: She sent a pre-emptive apology email to forestall the inevitable complaints about the delayed shipment.
The manager scheduled a one-on-one to forestall any rumors before the reorg was officially announced.

meanings.en: (of a group) difficult to control and prone to disagreement
meanings.zh: (团体)难以驾驭的;纷争不断的

meanings.en: easily irritated and prone to complaining or causing trouble; bad-tempered

examples: The toddler grew fractious around hour three of the flight, and so did everyone within five rows.
The fractious city council spent the whole meeting arguing over parking instead of the actual budget.

meanings.en: incapable of making mistakes or being wrong; never failing
meanings.zh: 绝不会错的;万无一失的(区别于 fallible‘会犯错的’)

examples: No trading algorithm is infallible, no matter how many backtests the sales deck shows.
My grandmother's dumpling recipe is infallible — I've never seen it fail, even at high altitude.

meanings.en: extremely small in size or amount, almost immeasurable

examples: The raise was so infinitesimal it barely covered the increase in her subway fare.
An infinitesimal delay in the algorithm's response time was enough to lose the trade to a competitor.

meanings.en: (of sound, especially a voice) sweet and smooth, pleasing to hear

examples: The podcast host has this mellifluous voice that makes even the ad reads sound like poetry.
Her mellifluous Cantonese lullabies were the only thing that got the baby to sleep on long flights.

meanings.en: to act as an official presiding over an event, especially a sports match or ceremony
meanings.zh: 主持;担任司仪/裁判(比赛、仪式)

examples: The retired referee agreed to officiate the charity match, even though his knees hadn't forgiven him for years.
Her uncle, ordained online for the occasion, officiated the wedding in the backyard under a string of fairy lights.
Three officials officiate every professional match, splitting the field into zones to catch offside calls faster.

meanings.en: the quality of being excessively eager to assert authority or offer unwanted help and advice

examples: The new HOA president's officiousness turned a simple trash-can rule into a three-page memo with diagrams.
Nobody asked for his officiousness at the potluck, but he still rearranged everyone's dishes by 'proper' order.

meanings.en: suggesting that something bad or unpleasant is about to happen

examples: The 'we need to talk' Slack DM from her manager felt ominous before she even opened it.
Ominous gray clouds rolled in right as we reached the summit, so we turned back without taking a single photo.

meanings.en: deliberately faithless or treacherous; deceitful in betraying trust

examples: His perfidious business partner secretly filed the patent under his own name the week before the deal closed.
History remembers him as perfidious, having secretly sold intelligence to both sides during the war.

meanings.en: (of a disease or condition) not responding to treatment
stubbornly resistant to authority or control; obstinate

examples: The refractory toddler refused every single vegetable on the plate, arms crossed like a tiny union rep.
After three rounds of chemo, the oncologist called it a refractory tumor and switched to a clinical trial.

meanings.en: unnecessary, especially through being more than what is needed

examples: The consultant's 40-slide deck felt superfluous when the whole recommendation fit in one sentence.
She donated three superfluous kitchen appliances she'd bought during the sourdough phase of lockdown.

meanings.en: (of weather or a place) uncomfortably or oppressively hot

examples: We stood on the sweltering subway platform for twenty minutes waiting for a delayed train with no AC.
The gym felt sweltering by 6 p.m., every treadmill occupied and the AC clearly losing the fight.

meanings.en: (of a person) pleasant and easy to get along with because of shared tastes or interests
meanings.zh: 意气相投的;友善随和的(区别于 genial‘泛指和蔼可亲’)

meanings.en: (of an environment) suited or agreeable to one's nature or needs

examples: Her new coworkers turned out to be surprisingly congenial, the kind of team that actually laughs during standups.
He found the quiet coastal town far more congenial to writing than the noisy apartment in the city.

meanings.en: to gather together in a crowd or group

examples: Delivery riders congregate outside the mall entrance every evening, phones propped up waiting for the next order.
Fans began to congregate outside the venue at dawn, hours before the doors even opened.

meanings.en: (statistics/data analysis) to break a whole or a combined data set down into its separate component parts
meanings.zh: (统计学/数据分析)分解;拆分(汇总数据)

examples: The analyst disaggregated the national unemployment figure by region and immediately spotted a rural spike nobody had flagged.
We disaggregated the churn dashboard by plan tier and found enterprise customers barely ever cancel.

meanings.en: to cause or give rise to a feeling, situation, or condition

examples: Constant last-minute schedule changes engendered a quiet resentment among the shift workers, though nobody said so aloud.
The CEO's transparent handling of the layoffs engendered a surprising amount of trust, even among those let go.

meanings.en: friendly, warm, and cheerful in manner
meanings.zh: 和蔼可亲的;友善的(区别于 congenial‘意气相投’,后者强调志趣相投而非普遍的和善)

examples: The genial bartender remembered everyone's order after just one visit and always asked about their week.
Despite the brutal quarterly numbers, the new manager stayed genial through the entire all-hands, cracking dad jokes to ease the tension.

meanings.en: pompous or extravagant speech or writing, especially intended to impress
meanings.zh: 夸张浮华的言辞(区别于 grandiose,后者指计划、风格等本身浮夸宏大)

examples: Strip away the grandiloquence in his pitch deck and the product is just a to-do list app.
The wedding toast was pure grandiloquence — twenty minutes of flowery praise before he even mentioned the couple's names.

meanings.en: impressively large, elaborate, or ambitious, often in an exaggerated or unrealistic way
meanings.zh: (计划、风格等)浮夸的;好大喜功的

examples: His grandiose plan to franchise the food truck to twelve cities fell apart after month two in the first city.
The renovation started with grandiose sketches of a rooftop pool and ended with a slightly nicer balcony.

meanings.en: done without good reason; uncalled for, especially something unpleasant or offensive
meanings.zh: 无端的;不必要的(尤指冒犯性的)

examples: Critics called the film's violence gratuitous, adding nothing to a plot that could've ended twenty minutes earlier.
His gratuitous comment about her weight had nothing to do with the project update she'd just given.

meanings.en: fond of company; sociable and enjoying being with other people

examples: She's the most gregarious person on the team, somehow knowing the name of every barista in a five-block radius.
Being gregarious made the coworking space feel less lonely, but it also meant he never got any actual work done before noon.

meanings.en: lacking any obvious organizing principle; done or chosen at random
meanings.zh: 无计划的;杂乱无章的;随意的

examples: His haphazard filing system meant the tax receipts were scattered across four different apps and a shoebox.
The move was so haphazard that boxes labeled 'kitchen' turned up in the bathroom three weeks later.

meanings.en: self-willed and obstinate, insisting on having one's own way

examples: Their headstrong toddler insisted on wearing rain boots to the beach and refused every other pair of shoes.
He's headstrong enough to quit a stable job for the startup idea everyone else called reckless.

meanings.en: very plentiful; produced or given in large amounts
meanings.zh: 大量的;丰富的(区别于 suffuse‘弥漫;充满’)

examples: He offered profuse apologies for the late delivery, along with a coupon nobody asked for.
By the third mile of the hike in that heat, we were all sweating profusely and regretting the extra layer.

meanings.en: moving backward, or reverting to an earlier and typically worse state
(astronomy) appearing to move backward relative to other bodies

examples: Cutting funding for the childcare program felt like a retrograde step after years of progress on parental leave.
Mercury goes retrograde again this month, and half my group chat is already blaming it for canceled flights.

meanings.en: resolutely and dutifully firm and unwavering in loyalty, purpose, or belief

examples: Her steadfast support got him through three rounds of layoffs at the company and the job search after.
Despite the market crash, he stayed steadfast in his monthly index-fund contributions instead of panic-selling.

meanings.en: (of a color, light, or feeling) to gradually spread through or over something
meanings.zh: (光线、颜色、情绪等)弥漫;充满(区别于 profuse‘大量的’这一形容词)

examples: Golden light suffused the office at sunset, making even the spreadsheet on her screen look almost pretty.
A quiet pride suffused the room when the interns' prototype actually worked on the first try.

meanings.en: the solemn or formal renunciation of a belief, cause, or claim, often under oath

examples: His public abjuration of the conspiracy theory came only after he'd lost half his followers and two sponsorships.
The contract included a formal abjuration of any future claim to the company's intellectual property.

meanings.en: to explain, discuss, or criticize something in excessive, tedious detail
meanings.zh: 过分强调;喋喋不休地讲(某事)

examples: I won't belabor the point, but the deck already covers page after page of why the budget doesn't work.
The performance review belabored one missed deadline for ten minutes and skipped six months of good work.

meanings.en: to describe, portray, or explain something precisely and clearly
to indicate the exact position of a border or boundary

examples: The onboarding doc delineates exactly who approves what, so no ticket sits in limbo for a week again.
The surveyor's map clearly delineated the property line, ending the years-long fence dispute between neighbors.

meanings.en: to cause someone to lose enthusiasm, hope, or confidence

examples: Getting rejected by eleven VCs in a row would dishearten most founders, but she just tightened the pitch deck and kept going.
Don't let one bad performance review dishearten you — ask for specific feedback and build a 30-day improvement plan.

meanings.en: (medicine/education) a learning disorder that impairs a person's ability to read, caused by difficulty processing written language
meanings.zh: (医学/教育)诵读困难症;阅读障碍

examples: The school psychologist diagnosed his dyslexia in third grade, after he kept reversing 'b' and 'd' on every spelling test.
She didn't realize she had dyslexia until college, when a professor suggested she try audiobooks instead of dense textbooks.

relatedForms.zh: 诵读困难的;患诵读困难症的

meanings.en: deriving ideas, style, or taste from a broad and diverse range of sources
meanings.zh: 兼收并蓄的;广泛涉猎的

examples: Her Spotify Wrapped was so eclectic — K-pop, death metal, and lo-fi study beats all in the top ten — that friends assumed she'd shared an account.
The new café has an eclectic menu that jumps from Sichuan mapo tofu to Neapolitan pizza, and somehow it works.

meanings.en: (medicine) chosen by the patient rather than urgently necessary
(education) an optional course that a student may choose to take

examples: Because the surgery was elective, the hospital pushed it back three weeks to free up beds for emergency cases.
He filled his last semester with electives — jazz history, wine tasting, and a pottery class — after finishing every requirement early.

meanings.en: excessively critical, finding fault in things that are minor or unimportant
meanings.zh: 吹毛求疵的;过分苛求的

examples: The code reviewer was so hypercritical that he flagged variable names in a one-line hotfix meant to ship in ten minutes.
Her hypercritical father found something wrong with every report card, even the ones covered in A's.

meanings.en: a person who regularly finds it difficult to fall or stay asleep
having chronic difficulty sleeping

examples: As a lifelong insomniac, she keeps three different white-noise apps on her phone for the nights nothing else works.
The sleep clinic finally gave the insomniac patient a diagnosis: chronic anxiety was keeping his cortisol elevated at night.

meanings.en: narrow-mindedness or isolation resulting from limited contact with other people or ideas

examples: After two years of remote work with the same five coworkers on Slack, he noticed his own insularity — nobody had challenged an idea of his in months.
Critics say the startup's insularity — hiring only from one university, ignoring outside user feedback — is why the product feels stale.

meanings.en: to intervene on behalf of another person, especially to resolve a dispute

examples: When HR threatened to fire her intern over a missed deadline, the team lead interceded quietly and got him a second chance.
My mom always interceded when my sister and I fought over the thermostat, texting both of us until we agreed on 72 degrees.

meanings.en: an abrupt remark inserted into a conversation
(grammar) a word or phrase expressing sudden emotion, used as an exclamation

examples: The grammar workbook listed 'ouch,' 'wow,' and 'ugh' as classic interjections that stand alone with an exclamation point.
Her sarcastic interjection during the budget meeting — 'sure, that'll fix everything' — got a nervous laugh from half the room.

meanings.en: to estimate or insert a value between two known data points
to insert a remark or passage into a text or conversation, sometimes altering its original meaning

examples: The AI note-taking app quietly interpolates missing words whenever the Zoom audio cuts out, which is great until it invents a sentence you never said.
Editors interpolated a footnote into the leaked memo before forwarding it, and nobody could tell which lines were the CEO's and which weren't.

meanings.en: to scatter or place things at intervals among other things

examples: She intersperses her Instagram feed with gym selfies and reposts of climate infographics so it doesn't feel like just another influencer page.
The professor interspersed the three-hour lecture with short YouTube clips, which was the only reason anyone stayed awake past minute forty.

meanings.en: having, showing, or done with good judgment or sense, especially in practical matters

examples: A judicious mix of index funds and a small crypto allocation is how her financial advisor described the portfolio — boring, but it survived the crash.
Judicious use of the mute button turned a two-hour all-hands into something she could actually half-listen to while answering emails.

meanings.en: (medicine) a substance that promotes bowel movements, used to relieve constipation
having the effect of loosening the bowels

examples: The gastroenterologist recommended a mild laxative for a few days rather than jumping straight to a colonoscopy prep dose.
Prunes have a well-documented laxative effect, something she discovered the hard way before a six-hour flight.

meanings.en: (philosophy) the branch of philosophy concerned with the fundamental nature of reality, being, and existence

examples: The seminar spent the whole afternoon on Aristotle's metaphysics, debating what it even means for something to 'exist.'
His thesis leaned heavily on metaphysics, questioning whether time is a real dimension or just a construct of perception.

meanings.en: the criminal offense of willfully telling an untruth after having sworn to tell the truth

examples: The witness's Instagram story, timestamped an hour before her alibi began, was enough for the DA to charge her with perjury.
Lying to Congress under oath isn't just embarrassing — it's perjury, and the executive's lawyers spent the weekend scrambling.

meanings.en: clever or skillful, especially in using the hands or in social situations

examples: Her adroit handling of the layoff announcement — no jargon, direct answers, a real Q&A — kept morale from collapsing entirely.
He's adroit enough with a wok to turn Tuesday's leftover rotisserie chicken into fried rice that tastes intentional.

meanings.en: to suggest or refer to something indirectly, without mentioning it explicitly

examples: In the all-hands, the CEO alluded to 'some difficult decisions ahead' without ever saying the word layoffs.
Her caption alluded to a breakup — 'new chapter, new city' — without tagging anyone, but everyone in the group chat knew who she meant.

meanings.en: comparable in certain respects to something else, typically for the purpose of explanation

examples: The onboarding coach compared learning the new CRM to learning a new phone — analogous enough that nobody felt dumb for asking basic questions.
Training a language model on biased data is analogous to teaching a kid using only one newspaper's opinion page.

meanings.en: to think deeply about something

examples: He spent the entire commute cogitating over whether to accept the counteroffer or take the new job's better title.
She likes to cogitate in the shower, which is why half her best product ideas show up in a voice memo at 7 a.m.

meanings.en: to erase or rub out completely, often a mark, memory, or feeling; also, to make oneself inconspicuous (self-efface)
meanings.zh: 抹去,擦除;(自谦)使不显眼

examples: No amount of scrubbing could efface the coffee ring the last tenant left on the countertop, so she just bought a runner to cover it.
He self-effaces in every meeting, crediting the whole team even when the fix was entirely his idea.

meanings.en: to make something clear by explaining it

examples: The onboarding doc doesn't elucidate how expense reports actually get approved, so new hires just ask in the help channel.
Can you elucidate why the API call fails only on Tuesdays? Nobody on the team can reproduce it.

meanings.en: to escape from or avoid someone or something, often cleverly
(of a fact, name, or idea) to fail to be remembered, understood, or achieved by someone

examples: The delivery guy eluded the building's broken elevator entirely by using the freight entrance everyone forgets exists.
Her name eluded him the whole conversation, even though they'd matched on the app three weeks earlier.

meanings.en: originating in the distant past, beyond memory or record (usually in 'time immemorial')

examples: Landlords have been raising rent right before renewal season since time immemorial, or at least since she moved to this city.
The recipe, passed down since time immemorial according to her grandmother, turned out to be a 1987 magazine clipping.

meanings.en: tending to talk a great deal; very talkative

examples: The Uber driver was so loquacious that she learned his entire divorce story before they'd even left the airport parking lot.
He's loquacious in Slack threads but goes completely silent whenever the camera turns on in a video call.

meanings.en: expressed clearly, easy to understand
able to think clearly, especially during illness or in a lucid dream
meanings.zh: 神志清醒的;(梦境)清醒的

examples: Her resignation email was refreshingly lucid — three sentences, no corporate softening, exactly why she was leaving.
The doctor said Grandpa was fully lucid during the video call, joking about the hospital food just like always.
He's been journaling before bed to try to have more lucid dreams, and honestly the app's success rate is questionable.

meanings.en: a general feeling of discomfort, illness, or unease whose exact cause is hard to identify; also a vague sense of dissatisfaction within a group or system
meanings.zh: (身体)不适感;(社会/经济)不景气,萎靡

examples: A low-grade malaise has hung over the office ever since the acquisition was announced — nobody's been fired yet, but nobody's relaxed either.
She woke up with a strange malaise, not sick enough to call in but too foggy to focus on the sprint review.

meanings.en: having or showing a wish to do evil or harm to others

examples: The anonymous review wasn't just critical, it was malevolent — clearly written by someone who wanted the restaurant to close, not improve.
In the finale, the assistant's chatbot turns out to be quietly malevolent, rerouting deliveries just to watch people panic.

meanings.en: to say harmful, often untrue things about someone; to slander
having an evil influence; harmful, especially in a subtle or dangerous way

examples: Former employees maligned the startup on Glassdoor so relentlessly that recruiters started asking about it in interviews.
The tumor's malign growth pattern meant the oncologist wanted to start treatment within the week, not after the family vacation.

meanings.en: to formally release someone from slavery; to emancipate

examples: The museum exhibit displayed the 1850s document by which a Virginia plantation owner manumitted eleven enslaved people in his will.
Historians debate why some owners manumitted enslaved workers only after death rather than while they could still claim credit publicly.

meanings.en: a professional soldier hired to fight for a foreign army or private group
motivated solely by a desire for money or personal gain
meanings.zh: 唯利是图的;惟利是图的

examples: The documentary follows a former mercenary who fought in three different civil wars before turning to private security consulting.
His sudden interest in her after the promotion felt mercenary — nobody texts that fast about someone with a smaller salary.

meanings.en: the complete destruction or removal of all traces of something

examples: The wildfire's obliteration of the entire hillside neighborhood was visible even from the satellite images the news kept replaying.
One bad update led to the obliteration of three years of customer data before anyone thought to check the backup logs.

meanings.en: to criticize someone sharply, especially from a position of authority
a sharp expression of disapproval or criticism

examples: The manager's public rebuke over the missed deadline — in front of the whole stand-up — was why two people started job hunting that afternoon.
The judge rebuked the lawyer for showing up late a third time, threatening contempt charges if it happened again.

meanings.en: to formally express disapproval of someone's actions, especially officially
a formal expression of disapproval, especially an official one

examples: HR issued a formal written reprimand after he cc'd the entire company on a complaint email meant for one manager.
The nurse received a reprimand for skipping the checklist, even though the patient was fine — protocol is protocol.

meanings.en: corresponding in size or degree; proportionate

examples: The offer letter promised a salary commensurate with experience, which turned out to mean 15% less than her last job.
His punishment felt commensurate with the mistake — a warning, not a firing, for one missed deadline.

meanings.en: a feeling of smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements, often leading to a lack of awareness of danger

examples: Three quarters of record growth bred a complacency at the company that left them completely unprepared when a competitor undercut prices overnight.
After passing the first two code reviews easily, his complacency showed — the third PR had a bug that took down staging.

meanings.en: (finance) to express or state a value in a specified currency or unit

examples: The bond was denominated in euros, so the fund had to hedge currency risk before booking the yield.
Most oil contracts are still denominated in US dollars, which is exactly why some exporters want an alternative benchmark.

meanings.en: to publicly declare something to be wrong or evil; to criticize harshly and openly

examples: The union denounced the new scheduling app within hours of its rollout, calling it surveillance dressed up as convenience.
She denounced her former business partner on LinkedIn, accusing him of forging the investor deck they'd used to raise seed funding.

meanings.en: the state of being famous, respected, or superior within a particular field

examples: She reached a kind of quiet eminence in the field — not famous outside academia, but every grad student cited her thesis.
His eminence as the go-to expert on tax law meant his newsletter got forwarded around every finance Slack in the city.

meanings.en: to absorb all of someone's attention or interest completely

examples: The new true-crime podcast engrossed her so completely that she missed her subway stop twice in one week.
He was so engrossed in the spreadsheet, trying to make the numbers reconcile before the 9 a.m. review, that he didn't hear his phone ring.

meanings.en: the great seriousness or moral gravity of something extremely bad; sometimes a monstrous or outrageous act (not simply 'great size')
meanings.zh: (性质)极端严重性;滔天罪行,暴行

examples: It took her a full week to grasp the enormity of the data breach — not just the numbers, but how many people's lives it touched.
Historians still argue about how ordinary citizens failed to register the enormity of what was happening next door.

meanings.en: deserving or causing public disgrace or shame; humiliating

examples: The startup's ignominious collapse — funds frozen, founder blocked on Twitter by his own investors — became a case study at three business schools.
He suffered an ignominious exit from the company, escorted out by security while his badge was deactivated mid-walk.

meanings.en: about to happen very soon — emphasizes closeness in time
meanings.zh: 即将发生的;迫近的(强调时间紧迫)

examples: The push notification warned of imminent flight delays two hours before anyone at the gate had heard a word from staff.
With the funding round's imminent close, the founders spent the weekend rewriting the pitch deck one last time.

meanings.en: about to happen, especially something unpleasant — emphasizes a looming, ominous sense hanging over the present, more than pure timing
meanings.zh: 即将来临的;迫近的(强调笼罩性的威胁感)

examples: The whole team could feel the impending layoffs before HR sent a single email — calendars kept clearing themselves overnight.
She couldn't shake the sense of impending doom every Sunday night, thinking about Monday's stand-up.

meanings.en: (of a place) unable to be captured or broken into; (of an argument or position) unable to be overcome or refuted
meanings.zh: 坚不可摧的;牢不可破的

examples: Their two-factor authentication setup felt impregnable until a single leaked recovery code brought the whole account down in ten minutes.
The debate coach built an impregnable case using nothing but the opponent's own quoted statistics.

meanings.en: harmful or hostile; unfavorable to something

examples: Constant Slack pings and four overlapping meetings a day are inimical to any kind of deep, focused work.
The new visa rules are inimical to the startup's plan to hire engineers from three different countries.
Her landlord's blanket no-pets policy felt inimical to half the building, which is mostly dog owners.

meanings.en: so good or unusual as to be impossible to copy or imitate
meanings.zh: 无法模仿的;独一无二的

examples: Her inimitable way of narrating a $40 Costco haul turned it into a two-million-view TikTok in a weekend.
The chef's inimitable trick of pairing street-food flavors with fine-dining plating made the pop-up impossible to copy.
He delivers bad news in his own inimitable style — a joke, then the layoff, then another joke.

meanings.en: a performer who acts using only gesture and movement, without words
to act out something using only gestures and facial expressions, without speaking
meanings.zh: 用手势/表情表演;做手势示意

examples: Unable to hear the directions over the drilling noise, the foreman just mimed 'turn it off' by slicing his hand across his throat.
The mime outside the museum followed a tourist's exact steps until the crowd burst out laughing and pointed it out to her.

meanings.en: massive, uniform, and rigidly resistant to change, especially of an organization or system
meanings.zh: 庞大一体的;整齐划一的;僵化的

examples: Migrating off the monolithic legacy codebase took the engineering team eighteen months and three near-mutinies.
New hires assumed the monolithic HR system would move fast on a relocation request; it took six weeks for a reply.
The union treats management as a monolithic enemy, even though half the directors actually agree with the workers.

meanings.en: no longer fashionable, useful, or accepted; outdated

examples: Her manager's outmoded belief that 'real work' only happens in the office clashed with the team's hybrid schedule.
The gym's outmoded cancellation policy still required a signed fax — in 2026.
Grandpa's outmoded advice to 'just walk in and ask for a job' hasn't applied since before online applications existed.

meanings.en: expressive gestures and body movements used instead of words to communicate
meanings.zh: 哑剧式表演;夸张的手势表演

meanings.en: (chiefly British) a theatrical entertainment performed at Christmas, based on a fairy tale, with music, comedy, and audience participation

examples: Every December, the local theater puts on a pantomime of Cinderella, and the kids scream 'he's behind you!' on cue.
Locked out of the meeting room with no phone, she resorted to pantomime through the glass door to explain she needed the projector.

meanings.en: surpassing all others; distinguished above the rest in a field
meanings.zh: 卓越的;首屈一指的;杰出的

examples: She's the preeminent voice on AI ethics on campus, quoted in every op-ed about chatbot regulation this year.
The clinic recruited the region's preeminent cardiologist, and the appointment waitlist tripled within a month.
In his preeminent position as lead reviewer, one thumbs-down from him can sink a restaurant's whole season.

meanings.en: a position that requires little or no work but gives status or income

examples: His uncle got him a board seat that turned out to be a total sinecure — one video call a quarter for a five-figure stipend.
Employees joked that the new 'Chief Culture Officer' title was a sinecure invented to keep the founder's old roommate on payroll.
She turned what everyone assumed was a sinecure into a full-time job, actually reading every report she was supposed to just sign.

meanings.en: modest and simple; not trying to seem impressive or important
meanings.zh: 不摆架子的;朴实无华的;不做作的

examples: The Michelin-starred chef still eats lunch at an unpretentious noodle stall two blocks from his own restaurant.
Her unpretentious apartment — thrifted furniture, bare walls — surprised guests who expected a funded founder's place to look glossier.
What I loved about the wedding was how unpretentious it was: a backyard, folding chairs, and tacos from a truck.

meanings.en: to make someone or something seem unimportant or of little value

examples: During her performance review, the manager belittled the six-month project as 'cute but pointless.'
Stop belittling his side hustle just because it's a food truck and not an app — he's out-earning you.
Her older brother had a way of belittling every acceptance letter as 'not that hard to get, really.'

meanings.en: extreme poverty; the state of lacking basic necessities

examples: After the medical bills wiped out their savings, the family slid from comfortable to near destitution in a single year.
The documentary follows gig workers one missed paycheck away from destitution, juggling three delivery apps just to make rent.
Losing the shop during the pandemic pushed them toward destitution before a GoFundMe from old customers pulled them back.

meanings.en: to speak of someone or something in a negative, belittling way

examples: The influencer got dragged online for disparaging a rival's skincare line while quietly using the same ingredients herself.
He kept disparaging remote work in meetings, even though his own team hadn't missed a deadline in a year.
She never disparages her ex to their kid, no matter how tempting it is after a bad custody weekend.

meanings.en: a great difference or inequality between two things

examples: The pay disparity between the two offices only came to light when someone leaked the spreadsheet in the company Slack.
There's a huge disparity between how smooth the app looks in the demo and how often it crashes for real users.
The disparity in commute times — twelve minutes for him, ninety for her — quietly decided which parent did school pickup.

meanings.en: not influenced by strong emotion; calm, objective, and impartial
meanings.zh: 冷静客观的;不带感情的

examples: The mediator stayed dispassionate through both parents' shouting, laying out the custody options like a checklist.
I need a dispassionate second opinion on this term sheet — my co-founder is too excited to see the red flags.
Her dispassionate tone while reading the layoff list made it feel worse, not better, than if she'd cried.

meanings.en: a deadlock; a situation with no apparent way forward

examples: Salary negotiations hit an impasse when the recruiter refused to budge above the original offer by even a dollar.
The roommates reached an impasse over the thermostat — one wants 65, the other 74 — and now there's a shared spreadsheet.
Talks over the custody schedule stalled at an impasse until the lawyers suggested splitting summer break down the middle.

meanings.en: showing or feeling no emotion; expressionless
meanings.zh: 面无表情的;无动于衷的

examples: The investor stayed impassive through the entire pitch, and the founder left with no idea whether it had landed.
Her face was impassive when the doctor read the test results, but her hands were shaking under the table.
He's impassive during every performance review, which somehow makes the good ones feel just as tense as the bad ones.

meanings.en: to make someone or something poor, or to deplete its resources

examples: Three straight years of drought impoverished the farming co-op, forcing half the families to sell their land.
Stacking five monthly subscriptions — streaming, cloud storage, a meal kit — quietly impoverishes people who never total the bill.
The overfishing off the coast has impoverished a fishing village that once exported to three countries.

meanings.en: bizarre or unfamiliar; extremely unconventional
meanings.zh: 稀奇古怪的;离谱的;怪异的

examples: His outlandish plan to pay rent in a token he'd minted himself somehow got two roommates to agree to a trial month.
The wedding planner pitched an outlandish theme — an underwater ceremony with rented mermaids — and the couple loved it.
Her outlandish claim that she'd cured her back pain with cold plunges and no doctor got 40,000 shares before a physician debunked it.

meanings.en: domineering; unpleasantly controlling of others

examples: Her overbearing mother-in-law rearranged the entire nursery while they were still at the hospital, 'just to help.'
The overbearing project lead rewrote everyone's client emails into his own tone before letting them send anything.
Being overbearing about the group project's font choice was, in retrospect, not the hill to die on.

meanings.en: a smallness of number or amount; a scarcity

examples: The paucity of affordable one-bedrooms near the office pushed half the new hires into a two-hour commute.
Reviewers slammed the app update for its paucity of features compared to the beta everyone had loved.
Given the paucity of evidence in the pitch deck, the VC asked for actual user numbers before the next meeting.

meanings.en: childish, immature, or silly, especially in a way unbecoming of an adult

examples: The CEO's puerile Twitter feud with a competitor knocked two points off the stock before lunch.
Their group chat descended into puerile nicknames and fart-joke GIFs about ninety seconds after it was created.
Calling your coworker's idea 'dumb' in front of the whole team was a puerile way to handle the disagreement.

meanings.en: quick, witty conversation or exchange of clever remarks
meanings.zh: 机智的应答;妙语连珠的对话

examples: The two podcast co-hosts' rapid-fire repartee is honestly the only reason anyone still listens.
Their first-date repartee over text was so sharp she screenshotted it to show the group chat.
He has no real repartee left for family dinners; every joke has already been made three Thanksgivings in a row.

meanings.en: violently split or divided, often by conflict (usually 'riven by/with')

examples: The startup was riven by infighting after the co-founders' public breakup, and half the team quit within a month.
Their family group chat stayed riven over politics long after the actual election had been decided.
The department, riven between the old guard and the new hires, couldn't agree on a single onboarding process.

meanings.en: a person who spends money in an extravagant, wasteful way
extravagant or wasteful with money

examples: His roommates call him a spendthrift over the $9 oat-milk lattes, but he's the one who always pays rent on time.
Her spendthrift habits — same-day online hauls, impulse concert tickets — finally caught up when the card got declined at checkout.
The grandfather set up a spendthrift trust so his notoriously extravagant grandson could only draw a fixed monthly amount.

meanings.en: to remove someone from a position of power, especially a ruler
to testify formally, especially under oath in a legal proceeding

examples: The board voted to depose the CEO after a leaked memo showed he'd known about the data breach for months.
Her assistant was deposed for six hours by opposing counsel before the harassment case even reached trial.
The generals who deposed the president promised elections within a year, which nobody in the group chat believed.

meanings.en: light, delicate, and translucent, especially of fabric

examples: She layered a diaphanous scarf over the swimsuit for the beach shoot, more suggestion than actual coverage.
The bridal shop's diaphanous curtains let in just enough light to make every dress look ethereal in photos.
Morning fog hung diaphanous over the trailhead, thin enough to see the sun but too dense to see the summit.

meanings.en: unable to be appeased, pacified, or changed; relentless
meanings.zh: 难以安抚的;不可平息的;不可动摇的

examples: Her implacable opposition to the merger turned every board meeting into a two-hour standoff.
The landlord was implacable about the late fee — no excuse, not even a hospital stay, moved him an inch.
He became her implacable rival the moment she got the promotion he'd been counting on.

meanings.en: to press or urge someone persistently, often to an annoying degree

examples: Recruiters kept importuning her on LinkedIn even after she'd said three times she wasn't job-hunting.
He importuned his parents for a down payment through the entire Thanksgiving dinner until they finally caved.
The startup's sales team importuned the same procurement manager weekly for four months before landing the contract.

meanings.en: impossible to restrain or hold back; irresistibly energetic
meanings.zh: 抑制不住的;难以压制的

examples: Her irrepressible enthusiasm for the project survived three rounds of budget cuts and a canceled launch date.
The toddler's irrepressible giggling during the solemn toast somehow made the whole room feel a little lighter.
He's irrepressible in meetings, cracking jokes even when the quarterly numbers are genuinely bad.

meanings.en: to place two things side by side, especially for comparison or contrast

examples: The exhibit juxtaposes AI-generated portraits with hand-painted ones, daring visitors to guess which is which.
Her Instagram grid juxtaposes glossy vacation shots with brutally honest captions about her anxiety.
The article juxtaposes the CEO's 'we're a family' memo with the layoff email sent two hours later.

meanings.en: relating to charitable giving; generous in promoting the welfare of others

examples: The tech billionaire's philanthropic foundation funds vaccine research, though critics say it's mostly a tax strategy.
Her philanthropic streak started small — a $10 monthly donation — and grew into a full nonprofit by thirty.
The company matches employees' philanthropic donations dollar for dollar, up to $500 a year.

meanings.en: to make someone less angry or hostile; to appease

examples: The airline offered a $50 voucher to placate passengers stranded overnight, which placated almost no one.
He tried to placate his sister by agreeing to host Thanksgiving, but she was still mad about the wedding toast.
Management sent a company-wide apology to placate staff after the surprise return-to-office announcement.

meanings.en: calm and peaceful; not easily upset or excited

examples: The lake stayed placid all morning, perfect for the paddleboard yoga class that always sells out on weekends.
He runs standups with this placid, unbothered voice — no matter how bad the outage is, it never changes.
Her placid response to the parking ticket surprised everyone; last time it happened, she cried in the car.

meanings.en: self-important; arrogantly grand in manner, speech, or appearance
meanings.zh: 自负的;浮夸的;自命不凡的

examples: The keynote speaker's pompous name-dropping made the whole panel cringe before he'd even reached slide two.
Her uncle gets pompous after two glasses of wine, lecturing everyone about wine regions he's never actually visited.
The reply-all email, full of pompous corporate jargon, could have just said 'the deadline moved to Friday.'

meanings.en: not securely held or positioned; dangerously likely to fall, fail, or collapse
meanings.zh: 不稳定的;危险的;岌岌可危的

examples: Freelance gig work leaves a lot of people in a precarious financial spot — a great month, then nothing for six weeks.
The ladder's precarious balance on the wet balcony tiles didn't stop him from climbing up for one more photo.
Her visa status is precarious enough that she avoids even minor traffic tickets.

meanings.en: an inclination or tendency toward a particular condition or behavior, often prior or inherited

examples: The genetic test flagged a predisposition to high cholesterol, so now she actually reads nutrition labels.
Growing up with an anxious parent gave him a predisposition to catastrophize every unread work email.
The therapist explained that a predisposition to burnout isn't destiny — it just means he needs firmer boundaries at work.

meanings.en: overstepping what is proper or polite; excessively forward or bold
meanings.zh: 冒昧的;放肆的;自以为是的

examples: It felt presumptuous to CC the CEO on a two-day-old support ticket, but the intern did it anyway.
Isn't it a little presumptuous to book a joint honeymoon before she's even said yes?
He forwarded his own performance review to HR with a presumptuous note asking for an early promotion.

meanings.en: the quality of having strong moral principles; honesty and integrity

examples: The auditor's reputation for probity was the only reason the board trusted the numbers without a second review.
Years of financial probity earned the credit union manager the town's trust — right up until the embezzlement scandal broke.
She built her whole personal brand on probity, so the leaked emails did more damage to her than to almost anyone else.

meanings.en: splendid and expensive-looking; lavish
meanings.zh: 奢华的;豪华的(尤指食物、装饰)

examples: The wedding planner unveiled a sumptuous ten-course tasting menu that blew through the couple's entire catering budget in one sitting.
Their new penthouse has a sumptuous marble bathroom with heated floors, the kind you only see in five-star hotel reels.
He booked a sumptuous suite for their anniversary, then spent the whole night stressing about the credit card statement.

meanings.en: to place one thing over another so both remain partly visible

examples: The photo app lets you superimpose a beach sunset onto any background, which explains half the vacation posts on her feed.
The architect superimposed the flood-zone map onto the site plan and realized half the proposed building sat underwater.
AI face-swap tools now superimpose one person's expression onto another's video in real time, which is equal parts impressive and unsettling.

meanings.en: likely to be influenced, affected, or harmed by a particular thing
meanings.zh: 易受影响的;易感的(疾病、情绪、劝说等)

examples: After three all-nighters finishing the deck, she was completely susceptible to whatever cold was going around the office.
Teenagers scrolling late at night are especially susceptible to targeted ads disguised as 'authentic' influencer recommendations.
He's always been susceptible to flattery, which is exactly why the sales rep opened with three compliments before the pitch.

meanings.en: a person who flatters someone powerful to gain favor

examples: Every all-hands meeting, the new hire turns into a sycophant, laughing at the CEO's jokes a beat too long and too loud.
The startup's board was full of sycophants who never once challenged the founder's wildly optimistic revenue projections.
She noticed the intern only agreed with whoever spoke last in the meeting — a textbook sycophant angling for a good review.

meanings.en: (of a desire, thirst, or feeling) impossible to satisfy or extinguish
meanings.zh: 无法满足的;不可抑制的(欲望、渴望等)

examples: After the marathon, his thirst felt unquenchable — he went through four bottles of water before he even reached the car.
The startup founder had an unquenchable curiosity, reading patent filings for fun on the weekends.

meanings.en: to accept or comply with something reluctantly, without protest

examples: Exhausted from arguing about the lease, David finally acquiesced and let his roommate keep the entire deposit.
She acquiesced to the landlord's rent hike rather than deal with apartment-hunting in this market again.
Rather than fight the new return-to-office mandate, most of the team quietly acquiesced and started commuting three days a week.

meanings.en: excessively eager to acquire money or possessions; greedy for gain
meanings.zh: 贪婪的;渴望占有财物的

examples: His acquisitive streak kicks in every flash sale — three new gadgets arrive before the last box is even unpacked.
The private equity firm's acquisitive strategy meant buying up struggling local chains one quarter after another.
Her acquisitive approach to her closet means a new haul every payday, whether she needs it or not.

meanings.en: formal or official approval; praise

examples: The junior analyst practically glowed after the partner nodded in approbation over her risk model.
On social media, approbation now shows up as likes, shares, and the rare verified-account reply.
He kept chasing his father's approbation long after he'd already built a company worth more than his father's entire career.

meanings.en: a person who aspires to achieve something, especially a position of distinction
meanings.zh: 有抱负的人;渴望成功者;候选人

examples: As a mayoral aspirant with almost zero name recognition, he spent every weekend knocking on doors in the district.
The gym floor is full of aspirant bodybuilders filming their sets for an audience that mostly isn't watching.
She was one of a hundred aspirants for the same product-manager role, so she led her resume with the one metric that actually moved.

meanings.en: having a strong desire to possess something that belongs to someone else
meanings.zh: 觊觎的;垂涎的(尤指他人之物)

examples: She shot a covetous glance at her coworker's corner office the second the promotion was announced.
Watching his old roommate's startup get acquired for eight figures left him quietly covetous of a life he used to mock.
The younger cousins grew covetous of the family cabin the moment grandma mentioned the will.

meanings.en: to cause someone to lose enthusiasm, hope, or confidence

examples: Three straight quarters of missed targets began to dispirit even the most optimistic members of the sales team.
The coach refused to let one bad loss dispirit the rookies before the playoffs even started.

meanings.en: inclined to argue or dispute; fond of arguing

examples: The family group chat turns disputatious every Thanksgiving the moment someone brings up politics.
He's the most disputatious person in stand-ups, questioning every estimate until the fifteen-minute meeting runs to forty-five.
Their book club got surprisingly disputatious over whether the ending was genius or just lazy writing.

meanings.en: not considered respectable in character, appearance, or conduct

examples: The apartment listing looked great until we found the disreputable landlord's reviews full of withheld deposits.
She bought the 'designer' bag from a disreputable reseller on Instagram, and it arrived smelling like glue.
He kept borrowing money from an increasingly disreputable list of payday-loan apps just to cover rent.

meanings.en: spoken or done without preparation or rehearsal

examples: When the projector died mid-pitch, she delivered an entirely extemporaneous version of the deck from memory.
His extemporaneous toast at the rehearsal dinner got more laughs than the one he'd spent a week writing.
The interviewer skipped the prepared questions and asked for an extemporaneous answer instead, just to see how he'd think on his feet.

meanings.en: (chemistry/materials science) a substance present in a material that reduces its purity or quality

examples: The mass spectrometer flagged trace impurities in the batch — just 0.02% sulfur, but enough to fail the pharma-grade spec.
Doping silicon with tiny amounts of boron introduces impurities that give the wafer its semiconductor properties.

meanings.en: stated or appearing to be true, but not necessarily so

examples: The ostensible reason for the layoffs was 'restructuring,' though everyone suspected it was really the failed product launch.
His ostensible purpose for the coffee chat was networking, but he clearly just wanted a referral.
The ostensible goal of the offsite was team bonding; the real goal, everyone agreed, was avoiding the office for two days.

meanings.en: to treat someone with hostility or cruelty, especially because of their race, religion, or beliefs
meanings.zh: 迫害;欺压(尤指因种族、宗教或信仰)

meanings.en: to harass or annoy someone persistently

examples: Employees who reported the harassment said they were quietly persecuted afterward, passed over for projects and excluded from meetings.
Throughout history, religious minorities have been persecuted and forced to practice their faith in secret.
Reporters persecuted the retired athlete with questions about the scandal every single time he left his house.

meanings.en: a trite, overused remark offered as if it were profound

examples: The manager's performance review was a string of platitudes — 'just believe in yourself,' 'growth takes time' — and zero actual feedback.
Her LinkedIn post about 'grinding through adversity' was pure platitude, liked four hundred times by people who skimmed the first line.
Instead of addressing the layoffs directly, the CEO's email leaned on platitudes about 'exciting new chapters.'

meanings.en: an attempt to make a false appearance seem true; a false show
a claim, especially a false or unjustified one, to some quality or accomplishment

examples: He kept up the pretense of being slammed at work just to dodge his in-laws' weekend visit.
Under the pretense of 'needing space,' she was already messaging someone new on a dating app.
The intern made no pretense of understanding the codebase and just asked for help right away.

meanings.en: conformity to accepted standards of behavior or morals; correctness

examples: HR sent a reminder about propriety at the holiday party after last year's karaoke incident.
Some coworkers questioned the propriety of the manager dating someone on his own team.
She kept a strict sense of propriety at work, never once venting about her boss in the group chat.

meanings.en: (of an animal) bred from parents of the same breed, with no crossbreeding
an animal of purebred lineage

examples: The breeder charged triple for the purebred Labrador puppies, papers and pedigree included.
The shelter mostly takes in mixed breeds, but every so often a purebred turns up without any papers at all.

meanings.en: complaining in a petulant or whining manner

examples: The customer sent a querulous email every single day the refund hadn't cleared, each one longer than the last.
His querulous tone about splitting the dinner bill made everyone regret inviting him.
By the third delayed flight, even the calmest passengers had turned querulous with the gate agent.

meanings.en: a state of calmness, stillness, or tranquility

examples: She finally found some quietude on the cabin trip, phone left in a drawer for three straight days.
The office empties out by seven, and a strange quietude settles over the open floor plan.
He credits early-morning runs, before the streets fill up, for the only quietude he gets all day.

meanings.en: to rebuke or reprimand someone, typically in a mild way
meanings.zh: 责备;告诫(语气通常较温和)

examples: The teacher gently reproved him for scrolling his phone under the desk during the lecture.
Her manager reproved her, calmly but firmly, for missing the deadline without a heads-up.
He reproved his little brother for leaving dishes in the sink again, though it never seems to stick.

meanings.en: to fail to resist pressure, temptation, or another negative force; to give in
meanings.zh: 屈服于;抵挡不住(压力、诱惑等)

meanings.en: to die as a result of an illness or injury

examples: After holding out through the entire meeting, he finally succumbed to the leftover birthday cake in the break room.
Running on four hours of sleep all week, she eventually succumbed to a nasty cold by Friday.
Her grandfather succumbed to the illness after a long fight, surrounded by family in hospice care.

meanings.en: to spoil, impair, or weaken the effectiveness or quality of something
to make a legal document or agreement invalid

examples: A single missing signature vitiated the entire contract, forcing both sides back to the negotiating table.
One overcooked ingredient vitiated what had otherwise been a flawless tasting menu.
The lawyer argued that the seller's undisclosed defect vitiated the sale agreement entirely.

meanings.en: a difficult or unpleasant situation; hardship

examples: The founder talked openly about the adversity of nearly running out of runway twice before the Series A.
She trained through months of adversity — a torn ligament, a canceled sponsorship — before finally qualifying for the marathon.
Losing both parents within a year was the kind of adversity that reshaped how he thought about work-life balance.

meanings.en: to make a wrongdoing seem less serious by providing partial excuses
meanings.zh: (为过错)找借口开脱;减轻(罪责)

examples: His lawyer argued extenuating circumstances: he'd been laid off that same week and missed the court date by accident.
HR weighed the extenuating factors — a family emergency, a broken-down car — before deciding not to fire him.
The professor wouldn't extenuate the late submission, even after hearing about the hospital visit.

meanings.en: done or said without previous thought or preparation
without preparation; spontaneously

examples: The whole team ended up in an impromptu meeting the moment the server crashed at 2 a.m.
What started as a quick coffee turned into an impromptu five-hour road trip to the coast.
With no notes and no warning, she had to speak impromptu in front of the entire board.

meanings.en: not harmful or offensive; harmless

examples: An innocuous comment about the budget spiraled into a forty-minute argument in the Monday meeting.
The email looked innocuous enough — just a shipping update — until the link turned out to be a phishing scam.
She meant it as an innocuous joke about his outfit, but he didn't speak to her for the rest of the shift.

meanings.en: (engineering/manufacturing) the quality of components being able to be substituted for one another without adjustment

examples: Standardizing bolt sizes across the product line gave the factory full interchangeability, so any warehouse could fulfill any order.
The whole modular furniture system depends on the interchangeability of panels, so a shelf from 2015 still fits a 2024 frame.

meanings.en: (of damage or loss) impossible to repair or put right
meanings.zh: 无法弥补的;不能修复的

examples: The leaked screenshots did irreparable damage to the influencer's reputation within a single afternoon.
Water pooled under the laptop overnight, and the technician said the motherboard damage was irreparable.
The argument opened an irreparable rift between the two co-founders, and the company split in two within a month.

meanings.en: many and various; of many different kinds
a pipe or chamber with several openings that channels fluid or gas, especially in a vehicle's engine

examples: Her reasons for quitting were manifold: the pay, the commute, the manager, the 9 p.m. Slack pings.
